breakfast.name: Fufu with Peanut Sauce
ingredients: Peanut sauce: 1 cup peanut paste, 2 tomatoes, 1 onion, garlic, palm oil, salt, chili pepper
instructions: Bring water to boil
Add cassava flour gradually, stirring vigorously with a wooden spoon
Stir constantly for 10-15 min — the fufu should pull away from the sides and form a smooth, elastic mass
Shape into a dome on a plate using a wet spoon
Make sauce: sauté onion and garlic in palm oil, add tomato, cook until soft
Stir in peanut paste diluted with water, add chili
Simmer 15 min until thick and oily on top
Serve fufu with peanut sauce alongside — tear pieces of fufu and dip
breakfast.description: Cassava fufu — the starchy foundation of Congolese meals. The pounding and stirring technique determines the texture: it should be smooth, elastic, and slightly stretchy.

breakfast.name: Vitumbula (Banana Fritters)
instructions: Mash ripe bananas to smooth paste
Mix with flour, sugar, salt, cinnamon
The batter should be thick enough to hold its shape on a spoon
Heat oil to 175°C
Drop spoonfuls of batter into hot oil
Fry until deeply golden on all sides, turning once
Drain on paper — they should be crispy outside, soft banana inside
Eat warm from the fryer
breakfast.description: Sweet banana fritters — sold by women at every Kinshasa market at dawn. The riper the bananas, the sweeter and more fragrant the fritters.

breakfast.name: Loso na Madesu (Rice and Beans)
instructions: Sauté onion and garlic in palm oil
Add cooked beans, mash some for creaminess
Add rice and water
Cook until rice is tender and has absorbed the bean liquid
The rice should be slightly pink from the beans and palm oil
Serve with fried ripe plantain
breakfast.description: Rice and beans cooked together — the combination is more than the sum of its parts. The bean starch gives the rice a creamy, pink-tinged quality.

lunch.name: Moambe Chicken
instructions: Season chicken with salt, brown in palm oil on all sides
Remove chicken, sauté onions and garlic until soft
Add tomatoes, cook 5 min until broken down
Return chicken, add palm nut cream and 1 cup water
Bring to gentle simmer — do not boil hard or the cream separates
Cook covered 30 min
Add okra, cook 10 more min
The sauce should be thick, oily, and orange-red
Serve over rice or with fufu
lunch.description: DRC's national dish — chicken braised in rich, oily palm nut cream. The moambe (palm nut pulp) gives a distinctive flavor found only in Central African cooking. Often called the 'butter of Africa.'

lunch.name: Pondu (Cassava Leaf Stew)
ingredients: 1kg cassava leaves (pounded smooth — this takes 30+ min by hand)
instructions: Pound cassava leaves in mortar until very smooth (or use pre-ground frozen)
Boil pounded leaves in water for 30 min — this removes bitterness
Drain, add fresh water
Add palm oil, onion, garlic, chili
Add smoked fish (flaked)
Simmer 20 min until thick and dark green
The oil should float on top when done
Serve with fufu — scoop fufu, dip into pondu
lunch.description: The everyday dish of the DRC — cassava leaves pounded for hours and slow-cooked with palm oil and smoked fish. Every Congolese person has eaten more pondu than anything else in their life.

lunch.name: Soso ya Mbika (Chicken in Pumpkin Seed Sauce)
ingredients: 2 cups pumpkin seeds (shelled, ground to paste)
instructions: Brown chicken pieces in palm oil
Sauté onions and tomato
Grind pumpkin seeds to a smooth paste — this is the sauce base
Dissolve pumpkin seed paste in warm water
Add to the pot with chicken
Simmer 30 min — the sauce thickens and turns pale green-grey
Season with chili and salt
Serve over rice or with fufu
lunch.description: Chicken in ground pumpkin seed sauce — the seeds give a rich, nutty, slightly earthy sauce unlike anything made with peanuts. A celebration dish in the Bas-Congo region.

dinner.name: Liboke (Fish in Banana Leaves)
instructions: Clean fish, score sides, marinate in lemon, salt, garlic, ginger
Lay banana leaves over heat briefly to soften
Place fish on leaves, top with tomato, onion, pepper, pili-pili
Add a splash of palm oil
Wrap tightly into parcels, tie with banana leaf strips or string
Grill over charcoal or steam 25-30 min
The banana leaf steams the fish and infuses it with a subtle green flavor
Unwrap at the table — the aroma when opened is the first course
dinner.description: Fish steamed in banana leaf parcels — a Congo River tradition. The wrapping technique traps all the juices, and the unwrapping at the table is a moment of shared anticipation.

dinner.name: Madesu (Stewed Beans)
ingredients: Fufu, rice, or chikwangue to serve
instructions: Cook soaked beans until just tender, 40 min
Sauté onions and garlic in palm oil
Add tomato paste, cook until it darkens
Add beans with their cooking liquid
Add smoked fish or dried shrimp for depth
Simmer 20 min until beans are very soft and sauce is thick
Season with chili and salt
Serve with fufu, rice, or chikwangue
dinner.description: Stewed red beans — cheap, filling, eaten almost daily. The palm oil and smoked fish transform simple beans into something deeply savory. The backbone of Congolese home cooking.

dinner.name: Sombe (Cassava Leaf and Spinach Stew)
instructions: Boil pounded cassava leaves 30 min to remove bitterness
Drain, add fresh water and palm oil
Add smoked fish, dried shrimp, onions, garlic
Add peanut paste dissolved in warm water
Simmer 20 min until thick, rich, and dark green
The palm oil should be visible on the surface — this means it's done
Season with chili and salt
Serve with fufu
dinner.description: Like pondu but richer — cassava leaves with peanut paste, smoked fish, and dried shrimp. Triple the protein, triple the umami. A feast-day version of everyday pondu.

snacks.name: Kwanga (Cassava Stick)
ingredients: Cassava roots (peeled, soaked 3-4 days until fermented)
instructions: Soak peeled cassava in water 3-4 days until soft and slightly sour
Drain, pound or press into smooth paste
Shape into cylindrical sticks
Wrap tightly in banana leaves
Steam or boil 30 min until firm
Cool — the sticks become dense and slightly chewy
Slice and serve alongside stews and sauces
snacks.description: Fermented cassava sticks wrapped in banana leaves — the slight sourness from fermentation is characteristic and intentional. Served alongside almost every Congolese meal.

snacks.name: Mikate (Congolese Doughnuts)
instructions: Mash banana, mix with flour, sugar, yeast, salt, warm water
Beat batter until smooth and elastic
Cover, let rise 1 hour until bubbly
Drop spoonfuls into hot oil
Fry until deeply golden brown all over
Drain — they should be light and airy inside
Eat warm, plain or dusted with sugar
snacks.description: Congolese doughnuts with mashed banana in the batter — the banana makes them moist and adds natural sweetness. Sold by the dozen at every street corner in Kinshasa.

snacks.name: Mikate (Congolese Doughnuts)
instructions: Mix flour, sugar, salt, nutmeg, yeast
Add mashed banana and warm water — batter should be thick but spoonable
Cover and let rise 1-2 hours until very bubbly
Heat oil to 170°C
Drop spoonfuls into oil — they puff into irregular golden balls
Fry until deep golden on all sides — 3-4 min total
Drain on paper
The banana gives them a slight sweetness and chewiness inside
In Kinshasa, mikate vendors appear at every intersection by 6am
snacks.description: Kinshasa's morning doughnut — fluffy fried balls with mashed banana in the batter for sweetness. The street vendors' rapid-fire frying technique and the mountain-pile presentations have gone viral as symbols of Congolese street food culture.

desserts.name: Grilled Pineapple
ingredients: 1 ripe pineapple (peeled, cored, sliced into rings)
instructions: Slice pineapple into thick rings
Sprinkle with brown sugar and cinnamon
Grill over charcoal until caramelized and marked, 3-4 min per side
Squeeze lime juice over
Drizzle with honey if desired
Serve warm — the caramelization intensifies the sweetness
desserts.description: Charcoal-grilled pineapple — the sugar caramelizes over the fire, creating sticky, smoky edges. Sold as street dessert across Kinshasa.

desserts.name: Beignets de Banane Plantain (Plantain Fritters)
instructions: Mash overripe plantains until smooth — they must be very ripe (black skin) for sweetness
Mix with flour, sugar, cinnamon, nutmeg
Drop spoonfuls into hot oil
Fry until dark golden — the natural sugar caramelizes
Drain and eat immediately
The exterior should be crispy-caramelized, the inside soft and sweet
desserts.description: Fried ripe plantain fritters — the plantains must be almost black for maximum sweetness. The caramelized edges are the best part.

drinks.name: Tangawisi (Ginger Lemon Drink)
instructions: Grate ginger, squeeze through cloth to extract juice
Mix ginger juice with lemon juice and sugar
Add cold water, stir until sugar dissolves
Adjust sweetness and ginger intensity to taste — Congolese drink it very strong
Add mint if desired
Serve over ice, very cold
drinks.description: Fiery ginger-lemon drink — Kinshasa's favorite refreshment. The ginger should burn your throat slightly. Believed to ward off illness and boost energy.

drinks.name: Kasiksi (Corn Beer)
instructions: Cook corn flour into porridge
Let cool, add sugar
Ferment 3-5 days
Strain and serve

drinks.name: Lotoko (Corn or Cassava Spirit)
ingredients: Distillation equipment (traditional: pot with condensation tube)
instructions: Ferment corn or cassava mash for 5-7 days
Transfer to distillation pot
Heat slowly — the vapor rises and condenses through a tube cooled with water
Collect the distillate — clear, strong, rough
The first and last portions are discarded (heads and tails)
The middle cut is lotoko — strong and fiery
Dilute if desired, or drink straight
drinks.description: Artisanal corn or cassava spirit — distilled in villages across the DRC. Raw, potent, and central to every celebration. Each distiller's product tastes different.
